html:
On this map in 300 CE, the western half of the Roman Empire is shown as the domain of Maximian, the co-emperor who ruled it under Diocletian's system of shared rule, the Tetrarchy. It covered Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain and western North Africa.

Diocletian made his fellow officer Maximian co-emperor, first as Caesar and from 286 as Augustus of the West. Maximian ruled mainly from Milan rather than Rome, close to the Rhine and Danube frontiers. In 293 the system grew to four rulers, and Constantius Chlorus became his junior emperor in charge of Gaul and Britain, where he ended the breakaway regime that Carausius had set up.

In 305 Maximian unwillingly retired alongside Diocletian. The four-way system soon broke down in civil wars, in which his son Maxentius seized Rome and Constantius' son, Constantine, won the West. Compare the eastern half: Rome under Diocletian.
